lesson.subtitle: Lesson 1 -- The Real Complaint
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Vitor (Mock Communicative) | Lesson 1 -- The Real Complaint

listenings.text: Welcome back to Front Desk, the podcast for people who run hotels. Today I want to tell you about the most useful complaint I ever received. A guest came down at eleven at night and told me the room was unacceptable. Her exact word. Unacceptable. Now, my first instinct was to defend the room, because I had checked that room myself that afternoon and it was fine. But I have learned something over fifteen years in this job: the first complaint is almost never the real one. So instead of explaining, I asked one question. I said, what happened tonight? And she told me. She had a video call with her team in Singapore at nine, and the internet dropped four times. She missed the call. By the time she came downstairs, the room had become the enemy, because the room was the only thing she could point at. The internet was the problem. The room was the messenger. Here is what I did. I did not apologise for the room, because the room was fine and she knew it. I apologised for the call she missed. Then I moved her to a room on the second floor, where the signal is strongest, and I gave her the direct number of our night technician. She wrote to me two months later to book again. So my advice is this. When a guest complains, do not solve the sentence they said. Find the sentence they did not say. Ask what happened, listen to the whole answer, and only then decide what to offer.

post_skill.title: What do you think?
items: "The room was the messenger." What does she mean by that?
Do you agree that the first complaint is almost never the real one? Does that match your experience?
She apologised for the call, not for the room. Was that the right call, or is it a risk?

language.title: These lines came from the recording. Match each one to the job it does.
words: "I completely understand why you feel that way."

defs: validates the feeling without admitting fault
tests a solution without promising it

language.text: Notice what is missing from this list: the word "sorry" on its own. Every line either asks, validates, offers or owns. An apology with nothing after it leaves the guest exactly where they were.

pre_comm.title: Reveal answer key
list: Just so I understand correctly, the problem started on Monday?
I completely understand why you feel that way. Tell me what happened.
What I can offer is two nights, and I can do that now.
Would it help if I moved you to the second floor?
I'll take care of it personally.
pre_comm.note: Accept justified variations. After each one, say it out loud and compare: which sounds more natural in your voice?

items: The setup
Your teacher is Claire, a guest who has just come down to reception at 10pm. She says the room is unacceptable. That is all she will say at first.
Information gap
Claire will answer ONLY as Claire, and only what you ask. She will not volunteer the real problem. Your job is to find it by talking to her — not by guessing.
Your goal
Leave the conversation knowing (1) what actually happened, (2) what she needs tonight, and (3) what you offered. Do not offer anything before you know the first two.

task1.label: Useful language
items: Just so I understand correctly...
What happened tonight?
I completely understand why you feel that way.
What would work best for you?
What I can offer is...
Would it help if...?
I'll take care of it personally.
I'm afraid that's not something I can do, but...
Second task — if time allows
Same guest, next morning. She is checking out and asks you to remove the room charge from her bill. Company policy says you can offer a discount, not a refund.
The tension
You want her to book again. You cannot give what she is asking for. Say no, and keep the relationship.

task2.text: Report back to your teacher afterwards: what did you say no to, and what did you say yes to?
